activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
Oliver had agreed to carry the microscope case only because the trail to the creek lab was flat and short, and because Ms. Wardak had promised that today they would finally see real cells. He did not despise science, exactly, but he despised worksheets where you had to label things you couldn't see. Cells were supposed to be invisible. Today they were going to catch one.

The class sat on logs beside the creek while Ms. Wardak handed out the onion, already sliced, and the little glass slides. Linda got her peel of onion skin onto the slide first and shoved Oliver aside to claim the microscope. "Careful," said Arizona. "Some of us still need to look." The two of them had been in a state of truce since the Great Bread Mold Incident in October, but it was a shaky one.

Linda squinted into the eyepiece and announced, "It's magnified fifty times. I read the knob, it says forty." Arizona crossed her arms. "Fifty times wouldn't even show a nucleus. It has to be way more than that." They looked ready to end the truce permanently, so Oliver, who had been quietly reading the side of the eyepiece, held up a finger. "The eyepiece says ten times. And the knob you turned says forty times, but that's the objective lens." He grabbed a stick and scratched it in the dirt: 10 x 40. "You multiply them. Ten times forty is four hundred."

Linda frowned at the dirt math. "So it's four hundred times?" "Total magnification," Oliver said, feeling the words click into place. "The eyepiece power times the objective lens power." Arizona looked through the eyepiece again, and her whole face changed. The onion skin had turned into a patchwork of neat brick shapes, each one outlined like a wall, and floating inside every brick was a small dark dot. "It's like a city," she breathed.

Oliver took his turn last, after jabbing his own thumb with the tweezers twice while peeling his slice of onion. Under the lens his cells arrived, wobbly and then sharp. He drew the brick shapes on his worksheet and labeled the outer line the cell wall, the thin line just inside it the membrane, and the dark dot the nucleus. His hands were shaking a little, but not from nervousness. He was laughing.

"Four hundred times," he said to nobody in particular. "I'm writing that in permanent marker on my hand."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Distracting, such as changing the subject or starting a new game, can interrupt teasing without challenging the teaser directly.
story:
The teasing had a schedule, Theo noticed, which was more than most things at Lakewood Middle School could claim. Every day at lunch, around the third bite of whatever the cafeteria was serving, a seventh grader named Denny would start in on Pierre's reading. Pierre read at lunch. He read during the walk to class. Once, famously, he had read through a fire drill. Denny found this hilarious in a way that never seemed to wear out.

Theo had been watching for a week, half by accident and then on purpose. He'd noticed something else, too. On Tuesday, a kid at the far table had stood up and yelled that someone's mac and cheese had rolled under the vending machine, and Denny's whole routine had collapsed like a bad soufflé. On Thursday, a dropped tray did the same thing. The pattern was almost systematic. Interrupt the moment, and the teasing couldn't restart, because restarting meant admitting you'd been teasing in the first place, and Denny was lazy about everything except his own reputation.

The problem was what kind of interruption to build. Theo had already tried the direct route in September, telling Denny to knock it off, and that had gone badly for Pierre, who got two extra weeks of "needs a bodyguard" commentary. So Theo needed something that wasn't a challenge. He thought about it through math, through gym, through Ms. Otieno's lecture on photosynthesis, which normally would have absorbed his entire brain.

The occasion arrived on Friday, because Friday was Aubrey's birthday and her mother had brought in a chocolate cake for the class party. Theo had made a small deal with Alycia: she would hold the cake box until his signal, and in exchange he would do her dishwasher duty for the weekend. They shook on it like it was a contract, which Theo's dad would have said was the only honest way to do business. Alycia, for the record, thought the whole plan was ridiculous, but she disliked Denny more than she disliked ridiculous plans.

At lunch, Denny leaned across the table. "Pierre, you reading the menu or the dictionary today? Hard to tell with you."

Theo knocked over his water cup. Not much, just enough. Alycia stood up with the box and said, loudly, that the cake was being cut right now and if anyone wanted a corner piece with actual frosting roses they'd better move. Half the table moved. Denny moved too, because Denny was not going to be the one kid without a rose. Pierre looked up from his book, blinked at the commotion, and got in line beside Theo.

"You planned that," Pierre said. It wasn't a question.

"Planned is a strong word," said Theo. "I'd say I had motivation."

Pierre closed his book, which for him was practically applause, and took the corner piece with two roses.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Theodore sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, a ruler, and a drawing assignment due Monday: a street scene in one-point perspective. He had drawn the road, the vanishing point, the buildings leaning in toward it. But when he stepped back to look, something was wrong. The street didn't feel like a street. It felt flat, like a wall with a road painted on it.

He stared at his lampposts, lined up along both sides. Every one of them was exactly the same height, exactly the same distance apart, like fence posts. Was that the problem? He remembered sitting in the car last summer, watching telephone poles whiz past on the highway. In his memory the faraway poles looked tiny, and the gaps between them seemed to shrink until they bunched together near the horizon. He had never wondered why. Now he wondered whether his pencil could do what his eyes did.

He erased every lamppost. Then he tried an experiment. First he drew the near ones tall, then each one after that a little shorter, and he squeezed the spaces between them tighter and tighter as they marched toward the vanishing point. His hand slowed near the middle of the page. What if he was overdoing it? He held the drawing at arm's length and squinted. The posts on the left side looked right, but the right side still looked stiff.

He called Rafaelle, who was already done with his own drawing. "Come over and bring yours," Theodore said. "Mine looks like the lampposts are standing in a police lineup." Rafaelle arrived ten minutes later with his sketchbook under his arm and his little sister's toy boat in his other hand, because he had been babysitting and had forgotten to put it down. The boat's rudder had come loose, which gave Rafaelle something to fiddle with while Theodore spread both drawings on the table.

Rafaelle's street worked. His lampposts shrank and bunched together in the distance, smaller and closer together the farther away they sat, even though they were all the same size in real life. Theodore laid his own drawing beside it and saw the difference immediately. His posts shrank but stayed evenly spaced, like buttons on a shirt. He grabbed the ruler again. "So the gaps have to shrink too," he muttered, "not just the posts." He measured Rafaelle's gaps with the edge of the ruler, not to copy the numbers, just to see the pattern. Then he redrew his right side, letting each gap close in a little more than the last.

His mother came by on her way to the sink and glanced down. "That looks like Elm Street," she said, which was more than she had said about anything he'd drawn all year. Usually she was indifferent to his art, in a kindly, distracted way. She pointed at the smallest lamppost, a sliver near the vanishing point. "You can barely see that one. How did you know to make it so small?" Theodore grinned. "Because far away things aren't just smaller. They crowd together too."

Rafaelle tapped the loose rudder on the toy boat against the table, thinking. "Drawing rules prohibit guessing, I guess. You have to measure." Theodore put his name in the corner, then leaned the drawing against the fruit bowl where the evening light caught it, the little street running all the way back to its single vanishing point. "One more lamppost," he said, and picked up the pencil again.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations are true for every number, such as 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), because both sides are the same expression written differently.
story:
The after-school tutoring room smelled of whiteboard marker and old pizza. Lucy spread out her worksheet and started on the problem Ms. Tanaka had circled twice: 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1). Solve for x. Her friend Maria slid into the next seat, chewing her pen like it owed her money.

"Divide both sides by two," Maria said. "That's the move, right? Whatever you do to one side, do to the other."

"Thanks, I was here first," Lucy said, but she tried it. Divide the left by two and she got x + 1. Divide the right by two and she got x + 1. She stared. Divide both sides again, subtract, it wouldn't matter. She crossed everything out and tried it the long way instead: distribute on the right, get 2x + 2 = 2x + 2, subtract 2x from both sides. The variables vanished. What remained was 2 = 2.

"Jeremi broke the worksheet," she announced, holding it up. "It says nothing."

Jeremi leaned over from across the table. "It says plenty. You just subtracted wrong."

"Subtract 2x from both sides yourself and watch." She handed him the paper. He worked it, frowned, worked it again, then tried a number at random. "Okay, x is five." He plugged it in. Ten plus two, twelve. Two times six, twelve. He tried zero, then negative three. Every single one worked. "This equation has no wrong answers," he said slowly, like the words were in a foreign language.

Lucy took the paper back and wrote a big check mark over the whole thing. She couldn't see x, couldn't pin it to one number, but she could test it, and the test kept passing. Maybe that was the answer: both sides were just the same expression wearing different clothes, so every number fit. She wrote across the top, "True for every number," and underlined it twice, then folded the page into a paper airplane and flew it across the room to Ms. Tanaka, who caught it without looking up from her grading.

Ms. Tanaka unfolded it, read it, and sent back the plane with a note pinned by a paperclip: "Correct diagnosis. Now please stop launching aircraft in my room. Also, your brother called the office. He says your lizard escaped again and he blames your 'hormones.' I told him you are the most competent thirteen-year-old I tutor and the lizard is on him."

Lucy read the note out loud. Maria laughed so hard she knocked over the marker tin. Jeremi picked up the last problem on the sheet, another equation, and started dividing both sides by two with the calm of someone who expected the worst. "If this one gives me 2 = 2," he said, "I'm becoming a poet."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: When a number inside a summed range changes, the SUM formula recalculates the total automatically.
story:
Sofia had until Saturday to prove that the school bake sale could afford a new soccer net, and the only computer she was allowed to use after school was the one in the back corner of the public library. She spread her crumpled list of sales on the desk beside the keyboard: twenty-seven items, each with a price, each written in her rushed handwriting. Her plan was to build a spreadsheet, add up the column, and turn the numbers into a bar chart so convincing that Coach would hand over the money on the spot.

Mr. Byrne, the librarian, wandered past with a cart of returns. "Sum formula," Sofia said, mostly to herself, pointing at her notes from class. "You type it, and it does the math for the whole column."

"Sounds like the machine's about to make your afternoon a lot easier," Mr. Byrne said, and kept rolling the cart.

She typed the prices into column B, one per row, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom and typed =SUM(B2:B28). When she pressed Enter, the number appeared instantly. She checked it by hand on scrap paper, adding in groups of five, and it matched. Her bar chart came out next: fat gray bars for cookies, brownies, lemon bread, all lined up like runners at a starting line. She leaned back, certain everything was finished.

That was when Caitlyn slid into the chair beside her, holding her own copy of the sales list. "Sofia. Jaxx says you wrote down his rice crispy squares wrong. He charged two dollars, not two twenty-five."

Sofia stared at row nineteen. She had indeed typed 2.25. "So my total's off by twenty-five cents," she said slowly, "and my chart bars are wrong too." She was already dreading redoing everything, because the deadline felt imminent; Coach wanted the numbers by Saturday morning, and it was Thursday.

Then she stopped. "Wait. Let me just test something." She clicked cell B19, deleted 2.25, and typed 2. Before she touched anything else, the total at the bottom of the column changed all by itself, dropping to the new number. She hadn't retyped the formula. She hadn't touched the total at all. It had simply updated.

"That's weird," Caitlyn said, leaning in. "You didn't redo the math?"

"I didn't redo anything. I changed one price and the SUM fixed itself." Sofia tried it again on a different row, changing a three to a four and watching the total climb by exactly one. She felt like a doctor who had made a diagnosis and then watched the symptom disappear. "It's a rule," she said. "When a number inside the summed range changes, the formula recalculates the total. Automatically." She copied the spreadsheet onto Caitlyn's flash drive as a backup, because losing it now would violate every rule of common sense.

The chart bars had shrunk too, still gray, still lined up. Sofia highlighted the cookie bar and turned it purple, Jaxx's favorite color, since his squares were the reason they'd caught the mistake at all. "Tell him the spreadsheet says thank you," she said, and hit print.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
Hailey's grandmother had sworn by her new ginger tea all weekend, telling anyone who would listen that it had chased away the worst headache of her life. Now Hailey stood in the science classroom after last bell, staring at a blank poster board that was due on Friday, three days away. Alison leaned over her shoulder.

"You could do the tea thing," Alison said. "Grandma drank it, headache went away, done. Easy A."

"It's one person," Hailey said. "That's a story, not evidence. But there might be something in it." She chewed her pencil. "Think about when she started the tea. She started it on her worst day."

Jocelyn, who was gluing sugar crystals onto her own project across the table, snorted. "Of course she did. Nobody tries a new remedy when they feel fine. Nobody says, 'What a lovely ordinary day, time for ginger tea.'"

"That's it!" Hailey grabbed Jocelyn's arm, and a sugar crystal fell off Jocelyn's poster and rolled under the sink. "Sorry. But that's it. A really bad headache day is unusual. What usually comes after something unusual?" She scrawled on the board: WORST DAY, THEN WHAT? "She might have felt better anyway, even if the tea did nothing."

"Ms. Campbell!" Jocelyn called, holding up her glue gun like a torch. "Does this have a name, or is Hailey inventing physics again?"

Ms. Campbell looked up from her grading. "Regression to the mean," she said, and went back to her red pen.

"See?" Jocelyn said. "You reinvented a real thing. You should be proud instead of terrified."

The next day, Hailey ran a test. She asked forty students to rate their mood from one to ten, picked out the ten who rated their day a three or lower, and gave five of them a "lucky pencil" while the other five got nothing. By afternoon, she collected the ratings again. The lucky-pencil group had climbed to mostly sixes and sevens. So had the group with nothing. Both groups floated back toward ordinary. She took the results home and, feeling a small rebellion against her grandmother's certainty, taped them onto the poster board anyway.

At the fair on Friday, her grandmother stopped in front of the display and read it twice, her lips moving. Then she laughed so loudly that the boy demonstrating volcanoes at the next table spilled his baking soda.

"So the tea might not be a miracle," her grandmother said. "Fine. I still cherish it. It's warm and it tastes like someone cares."

Hailey hugged her. "Drink it forever. Just let the data live too."

Ms. Campbell pinned a blue ribbon to the corner of the poster, and Hailey stood there grinning while her grandmother went straight home, she declared, to make a spontaneous pot for the whole judging committee.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, including weekends, helps keep the body's internal clock, called the circadian rhythm, steady.
story:
Madison kept a tally in her notebook: three nights at Camp Wawasee she had woken up with her heart slamming like a woodpecker on a tin roof. The first time she blamed the raccoon that raided the snack bin. The second time she blamed Tyler, who had told a story about a canoe ghost right before lights out. By the third time she was out of blame targets, so she started writing down everything she could remember instead. She had gone to bed at eleven, woken up at seven, then caught up on sleep Saturday morning until almost noon. Sunday she had done the same thing.

"You're doing science on your own face," said Cedrick, peering over her shoulder at breakfast. "That's kind of amazing and kind of sad."

"I'm doing science on my sleep," Madison said. "Monday nights are the bad ones. Saturdays I sleep in. Those facts might be friends."

She was starting to speculate. Maybe the sleeping in was the hidden cause, the raccoon and the ghost story just decoys. It would explain why the bad mornings came after the lazy ones, like a bill arriving after the party.

She needed more data, so she recruited Cedrick and Tyler, since misery apparently loved witnesses. "New rule," she announced. "I go to bed and wake up at about the same time every day, weekends included. You two are my control group. Keep being your normal chaotic selves."

"Thanks," said Tyler. "Being a control group is my dream."

The first Saturday, waking at seven felt like a personal insult, but Madison did her breathing trick anyway, four counts in, slow let out, while Cedrick stood at her bunk doing it wrong on purpose, puffing like a dragon with allergies. She threw a pillow at him. She still got up.

Monday morning arrived, and her heart behaved like a normal heart. No woodpecker. No tally mark. She checked twice, because one quiet morning could be luck. The second weekend, she held the line again, and Monday morning came up smooth as the lake at dawn.

She reported her findings to Mr. Hoffmann, the nature instructor, who was cleaning the frog tank. "So there's a thing called the circadian rhythm," she said. "It's your body's internal clock, and keeping your bedtime and wake time steady every single day keeps it steady too. I tested it on myself. With witnesses."

Mr. Hoffmann raised an eyebrow. "You did your own experiment? At my camp? During frog season?"

"The frogs were the control group too," said Cedrick solemnly, holding up a bullfrog.

"That's Tyler's frog," said Tyler. "Give him back."

Madison wrote one last line in her notebook, closed it, and carried it down to the lake, where the water lay flat and calm, like a Monday morning that had finally decided to cooperate.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Victor had a math test on Friday, and his mother had just told him there was no money for the salmon she'd seen in the store ad. That would not have mattered except for the headline glowing at him from the family laptop: "Kids Who Eat Fish Twice a Week Score Higher on Tests." He read it three times, then copied the link into a message to Malachi.

"Check this," he typed. "If it's true, I'm sunk."

Malachi replied with a shrug emoji, which was no help at all, so Victor dug into the article himself. It described a study of thousands of students, and it was careful to say the fish eaters scored higher. It did not quite say the fish caused the higher scores, though the headline came close. Victor opened a new tab and started reading about how studies like this worked.

At school the next day he cornered Malachi at the lockers. "You know what I figured out last night? Ice cream sales and sunburns both go up at the same time every year, but ice cream doesn't burn you. Hot weather causes both. So two things rising together might both be caused by something else."

Malachi chewed on that. "Okay, but what else would fish kids and good-grade kids have in common?"

"That's the test," Victor said. "I want to verify it. If I can find what else those students share, I'll know whether the fish matters."

At lunch they sat with Lea-Rose, whose father was a diplomat and whose family had lived in three countries. She listened to the whole plan while pushing rice around her tray. "In Japan we ate fish constantly," she said. "And I did fine. But my parents also made me do homework the second I got home, every single day, no excuses." She paused. "Actually, in every country, that was the rule. The fish changed. The homework rule never did."

Victor felt the ground shift a little. He went home and found the original study. The fish eaters were also more likely to have parents who read to them, lived in houses with more books, and ate dinner at a regular table. Fish was expensive; the families buying it tended to have money for other things too. He wrote it all down, then leaned back, torn between triumph and something heavier. He had uncovered a real idea, and it had cost him the easy fix. There was no fish magic coming on Friday.

His neighbor Mr. Holloway was watering his mums when Victor dragged the recycling bin in, and Victor explained the whole thing, ice cream and sunburns included. Mr. Holloway nodded slowly. "My mother swore oatmeal made her children honest," he said. "We were just afraid of her."

On Thursday night there was no fish in the house, so Victor made his own dinner of toast and a banana, and after the dishes he sat at the laptop and did practice problems until his eyes burned. When his mother came home late from her shift, she glanced at the screen and then at him.

"What's all this?"

"Just my homework," Victor said. "It turns out that part was never about the fish."

She looked like she wanted to ask more, but she was too tired, and the toast was cold anyway. He slid half of it across the table to her, and she took it.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
The group chat lit up the moment Carter's mom left for her dinner. It was the neighbor, Ms. Tan, checking in from her own night out. "How's my girl? Bath at seven, pajamas by seven thirty." Carter typed back a thumbs-up, then a second one, because one felt too casual for a first babysitting job. Down the hall, three-year-old Poppy sat in the tub, patting the water while Carter crouched beside it with his sleeve rolled up like a proper lifeguard.

"Water goes to the equator," Carter announced, pointing at the line he'd drawn in his head around the middle of the tub. "Halfway. No higher." His mom had drilled it into him all week, along with the part that had surprised him most: a little kid could drown in just a few inches of water, and there wouldn't be any splashing or crying out to warn him. So the rule was absolute. Never alone, not even for a second, not in the tub and not next to it.

Then the phone rang. The screen said "Family Chat," and behind the name the chat was already flooding: Nelson asking if Carter had survived, Adem sending a picture of his own dinner, his mom's name flashing with an actual call. Carter stood up, and Poppy looked up at him with big eyes, clearly calculating whether she was about to be abandoned. "Nope," he said. He grabbed the dinosaur towel, lifted her out dripping, and wrapped her into a squirming burrito. "You come with me. House rule." He answered the call with a soggy toddler on his hip.

"So nothing's on fire?" his mom asked, laughing at the towel. Behind her voice, Nelson had typed "WHO IS THAT," and Adem had sent three fire emojis. Carter turned the camera so Poppy could wave, and his mom's face did something complicated, soft and sharp at the same time. "You took her out of the bath to answer the phone." It wasn't quite a question, and underneath it Carter heard the real one: had he thought of that himself, or had he been about to leave her?

"I'll confess," Carter said. "At first I almost stepped into the hallway. Then I remembered you saying kids can go under quiet, no splashing, no yelling, even in barely any water. So she came along." His mom was quiet for a second, which in the Tan family group chat meant something big. "That's not the conventional way to answer a phone," she said, "but it's the right way."

Poppy sneezed, dripping onto Carter's sock, and pointed at the screen. "Do it again," she commanded. "Do the towel again."

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: The stage direction exit is Latin for "he or she goes out," and exeunt is Latin for "they go out," used when two or more characters leave.
story:
The air conditioning in the public library was broken, and by three o'clock the study room felt like a greenhouse. Joshua wiped his palms on his jeans and stared at the photocopied page Ms. Haddad had given him: Act III, scene one of Julius Caesar, all those long speeches marching across the paper in columns. His assignment was to paraphrase each speech into modern English, and so far he had managed exactly one line. Brutus says Rome is more important than friendship became, somehow, three scribbled words in his notebook.

Chace slumped into the chair across from him. "I only came for theWi-Fi," he said, "but my mom says I have to stay until five." He wanted to finish his math worksheet fast so he could watch a soccer video before dinner, and he kept glancing at the clock on the wall. Malak arrived last, hair damp from the humid walk over, carrying a bag of pretzels she immediately had to put away because of the no-food sign.

"Okay," Joshua said. "Help me with one speech and I'll help you with fractions after." Chace dragged his chair around, which was progress, since he had spent the first ten minutes insisting Shakespeare was impossible. Malak read over Joshua's shoulder, her finger tracking the lines. Casca spoke, then Cassius, then Metellus Cimber, and each time Joshua turned the old words into new ones. "You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things" became "you're not even listening, you're basically furniture."

Then he hit the bottom of the scene. One word, in italics: Exeunt. Earlier, when Casca left alone, the script said Exit. Joshua frowned. He flipped back, checked, flipped forward again. Every single departure was exit, except this one, and this was the only moment where the whole crowd left at once. "Wait," he said slowly. "Exit is when one person goes out." He pointed at the word on the page. "So exeunt must mean they go out. Plural. The Latin has two versions."

"Prove it," Malak said, because she was the kind of person who never took an answer on faith. They turned to the library's big Shakespeare volume and hunted through three more plays, and every crowded exit ended with that same word. Chace, who had abandoned his worksheet entirely, started reading stage directions aloud in a dramatic voice, announcing "Exeunt all" whenever anyone so much as stood up to sharpen a pencil.

When Ms. Haddad came by to collect the room key, she found the three of them redrafting Cassius's speech about ambition in words a sixth grader could actually say out loud, distributing the long sentences among themselves like actors splitting a script. She paused at the door, listened for a moment, and said, "Tuesday, then, same room." Joshua wrote it on his hand so he wouldn't forget, and underneath it, just the word exeunt.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
story:
Riley had read the same sentence in her charter handout eleven times, and it still sounded like it had been written by a robot with a law degree. Mr. Mensah wanted each of them to explain one right in their own words by Friday, and her right was dignity, which was the problem, because she could not figure out what it actually meant. She had planned to copy the dictionary definition and hope for the best, but Audrey had already tried that trick in September and Mr. Mensah had written "in whose words?" across it in red pen.

At lunch she spread the handout on the table next to Audrey's pudding cup. Athena slid in across from her, still holding her phone.

"I'm doomed," Riley said. "I picked dignity because it was the first word and now it's the vaguest word."

"Wait." Athena put the phone down. "My cousins live in Germany, and we had this argument at Christmas. Their constitution starts with dignity too. Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, which they've had since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'"

"Inviolable," Audrey repeated, testing it. "That's a robust kind of word."

"That's the thing," Athena said. "It's their constitution, and the very first sentence is about dignity. First. Before anything else."

Riley looked down at her handout, at Canada's own first article, the one guaranteeing rights and freedoms subject to reasonable limits. One country led with dignity like it was the whole point. The other listed rights and then immediately said well, mostly. She turned that over while Audrey stole a cracker.

"So here's my idea," Riley said. "If Germany puts it first, maybe the order tells you something. Like what a country thinks matters most before it starts making excuses." It was a pattern she couldn't see directly, only test. She wrote two columns in her notebook: first words on one side, limit-clauses on the other.

By Friday she had a paragraph she actually believed in. She stood up, said dignity meant nobody could treat you like a thing, like something you could use up and throw away, and that a country that made that sentence one of its very first had picked a side. Mr. Mensah read it twice, which he almost never did.

"In whose words?" he asked.

"Mine," Riley said. "Mostly. Athena's cousins helped."

He handed it back, and at the bottom, in red pen, it said just one thing. "Sustain this. You're on to something."

Riley sat down and immediately started planning her next paragraph, because her motivation, previously located nowhere, had finally shown up to class.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Isabelle climbed Kalia's front steps carrying the shoebox under her arm like a bomb that might go off. Inside the box was the group project for science club, and the group was already arguing through the screen door. She could hear Ian insisting the habitat model had to have a waterfall, and Kalia saying there was no room for a waterfall because the cave took up the whole back half.

"The cave goes," Ian said when Isabelle walked in. "It's ugly."

"You haven't even seen the whole thing," Kalia said. "You only built the cave. I made the rest."

Isabelle set the box on the kitchen table between the bowl of popcorn and Kalia's cat, who was watching everything with narrow, judgmental eyes. Each of them had built a section at home, in secret, because they had thought surprises would be fun. Now the surprises were at war. Ian's cave was gray and crumbly. Kalia's river valley was green and detailed. Isabelle's own piece, a rocky slope with a family of paper lizards, looked like it belonged to a different planet entirely.

"You put lizards in a river valley?" Ian said. "Ms. Bekele is going to think we made three projects and smashed them together."

"That's exactly what we did," Isabelle said. She was quiet for a moment, turning a lizard in her fingers. She remembered the story her grandfather had told her last summer, from ancient India, about the blind men and the elephant. Each man touched one part, the trunk or the leg or the ear, and each described the animal completely differently, because each had felt only his own piece. She had thought it was just an anecdote to make her laugh, the way her grandfather told it, with the man holding the tail insisting an elephant was like a rope. Now she looked at the shoebox and felt the pieces click together in her mind.

She held up the tail-shaped piece of paper. "Okay, listen. Blind men, elephant, ancient India. Each one touches a different part and describes it completely differently. Sound familiar?" She pointed at the cave. "That's a leg." She pointed at her slope. "That's an ear."

"So the elephant is our project," Kalia said slowly, "and we're all being the blind men."

"We've each only seen our own part," Isabelle said. She pulled the box apart gently, section by section, and laid them out so all three could walk around the table and see everything at once. Ian circled twice, chewing popcorn, and stopped at her paper lizards.

"Those aren't lizards," he said. "Those are clearly tiny venomous dragons."

"They're lizards, and they contribute to the ecosystem," Isabelle said, "but fine, we can label them Komodo dragons if it makes you happy."

They rebuilt the habitat together, moving the cave to the edge where the ugly gray looked like a cliff, threading the river past Isabelle's slope so the dragons had somewhere to drink. By the time the porch light came on, the model looked like one world instead of three. Kalia's mom called from the hallway that pizza had arrived, and Ian lifted the box carefully to the counter.

"Same time next week?" he asked. "Everyone builds their piece together, in the same room."

"Same room," Isabelle said, "and nobody touches the elephant alone."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
George was sitting cross-legged on Owen's bedroom floor, phone balanced on his knee, when Owen's little brother barged in holding a tablet like it had betrayed him. "It won't let me in," the kid said. "I put my birthday in three times and it just keeps asking again."

George leaned over. The screen showed a signup page for the app everyone at school used, and the birthday field was outlined in red. "What'd you type?" he asked.

"March fourth, 2014."

Owen laughed from his bed, but George didn't, because something clicked. He remembered back in September, when Fatimah had turned thirteen and come to school glowing, waving her phone around, saying her dad had finally let her make an account. At the time George had thought her dad was just strict. Now he watched the little brother try again, watched the red outline appear again, and a pattern assembled itself in his head. "It's not broken," George said slowly. "It's checking. How old are you?"

"Eleven."

"There's a law," George said, mostly to test the idea out loud. "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, from 1998. Websites can't collect your personal information if you're under thirteen unless your parents say yes first. That's why the app wants your birthday. It's not being annoying. It's being legal." The kid tried typing a different year, 2010, and the page jumped ahead instantly, asking for an email. George pulled the tablet back before he could go further. "That's lying to it, though. That's not the same as being allowed."

The kid stormed out. Owen shrugged. "He'll just do it at school."

George opened a message thread on his phone and typed to Fatimah: is it true you couldn't get an account till you were 13? She answered fast: yep, dad showed me the rule. sites have to get parental consent before they collect info from kids under 13. felt unfair at the time. still kind of does.

George typed: tonight my cousin tried faking his birthday. i stopped him. She sent back a thumbs up and then: you sound like my dad.

He put the phone face-down on the carpet. Outside, a streetlight buzzed on, and somewhere down the block a dog barked at whatever nocturnal things moved along the fence line. Owen tossed him a controller and said they might as well play something before his mom made them turn everything off, before the no-screens curfew that Owen complained about every time and never actually refuted, because it always won.

They played two rounds. George kept thinking about the little brother, alone in the next room, tapping at that red birthday box in the dark. Somewhere in the house a door clicked shut.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
On Monday, Mr. Hussain taped a sign to the auditorium door: IMPROV TRYOUTS, FRIDAY, 3 P.M. NO SCRIPT, NO CANCELLING. Jonathan read it twice, then Alisha bounced up beside him and said, "We're doing this together, right? You, me, one scene, glory."

The trouble was that improv had rules nobody had written down. On Tuesday, Alisha held her hands out like she was gripping a fishing rod, reeled in an invisible fish, and said, "Nothing bites today, Grandpa." Jonathan, standing right there on the stage, replied, "Hi, I'm your neighbor, here to borrow sugar." Alisha lowered her hands slowly. "Jonathan. I was fishing."

That night he texted his cousin, the one who actually did improv. The reply came as a message he read three times: "An offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem. She gave you a lake, a family, a bad day. You ignored all three and invented a kitchen. Never do that. Say yes to the offer, then add to it." Jonathan lay on his bed staring at the ceiling. So a fishing rod wasn't just a fishing rod. It was a whole argument about where they were, and he had flattened it.

Wednesday, he tested his idea. Alisha started a scene by clutching her throat and gasping, "The cafeteria chili, Principal whoever, it was the chili." A chili, an authority figure, a mystery: three offers, all sitting there waiting. "Yes," Jonathan said, diving in, "and I saw Coach sneak in a second helping, so whoever made it must be somebody important." Alisha grinned so wide he could see her back teeth. "The nurse," she whispered. "The nurse made the chili." They were both laughing before the scene ended.

By Thursday they could run a scene about alien substitute teachers without collapsing, mostly. Finley, watching from the third row, shouted suggestions like "penguin detective" and then complained when they ignored him. "You can't violate your own premise," Jonathan called down. "We're teachers, not penguins." Finley said that was the most legitimate excuse he'd ever heard and threw a rolled-up program at the stage.

Friday at 3:02, Mr. Hussain pointed at the two of them and said, "Go." Alisha picked up an invisible suitcase, hefted it like it was heavy, and said, "The last train leaves in five minutes, and you still owe me an apology." Jonathan took the suitcase from her, staggered under its weight, and said, "Yes, and here's the ticket I bought you, because I'm coming too." In the second row, Finley cupped his hands around his mouth and yelled, "BEST ONE YET."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
story:
"Mark your calendar for the fourteenth of February," Nicholas's mother called from the kitchen, "because this year the dinner lands on Valentine's Day, of all things." Nicholas stopped halfway up the stairs. He had already promised Ms. Dela Cruz that his culture project would be built around the family's Lunar New Year dinner, and he had written February fourteenth in his planner in big blue letters. Last year it had been later in February. Or was it January? He dug through his backpack for the old planner and found last year's entry: the dinner had been in late January, not February at all.

He called Teagan first. "Quick question. Is Lunar New Year always on the same date?" Teagan, who celebrated it too, laughed at him through the phone. "No, that's the whole point. It falls on a new moon between January twenty-one and February twentieth. That's why it jumps around." Nicholas copied the words into his notebook, then checked a second source, then a third, because Ms. Dela Cruz would want proof. Every source said the same thing, and every country his family claimed, China on his dad's side, Vietnam on his mom's, kept the same moving date. His project idea suddenly felt shakier. He couldn't schedule interviews, photos and a cooking demonstration around a date he couldn't pin down, and worse, he couldn't explain why it moved.

At the dinner itself, steam fogged the windows and the whole apartment smelled of ginger and scallions. His uncle, a veteran of these feasts who had cooked the dumplings for thirty years, kept the platters coming while Nicholas's little cousins chased each other between chairs. Long noodles curled in a tureen; his grandmother said they symbolize long life, and everyone at the table slurped them extra slowly on purpose, even the cousins, who giggled through it. Nicholas balanced his camera on a stack of books and filmed the whole parade of dishes.

Then he noticed something. His grandmother had a paper calendar on the fridge with tiny moons printed on every date, and the full circles and empty circles marched in a perfect parallel line down the page. He counted forward from the new moon, then backward, then flipped the pages of two more months. The pattern held. He ran the counting test in his notebook right there at the table, using dates his mother remembered from past dinners, and every single one matched a new moon. The rule wasn't random. It was a pattern you could follow, like footprints.

"So my project isn't about a broken calendar," he told Teagan on the phone later, bouncing a tennis ball off his bedroom wall between sentences. "It's about a different clock running alongside ours." He reorganized his poster that night, laid out three years of dinners with their moons, and titled it with a fat marker.

On presentation day, Ms. Dela Cruz stopped at his poster the longest. She tapped the row of empty moon circles and looked up at him with raised eyebrows. Nicholas grinned and uncapped his marker. "Want to see what happens next year?"

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: In northern summer, the rainy band of rising air near the equator, called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, shifts north over South Asia and helps bring monsoon rains.
story:
Wyatt spread two satellite images across the library table like a pair of mismatched postcards. January on the left, July on the right, both showing South Asia from space. His science presentation was due Thursday, and so far all he had was a title, "Monsoons and Rice," and a feeling that he was missing something obvious.

"You've been staring at those for twenty minutes," Orion said, sliding into the chair across from him. "What are we looking at?"

"Clouds. In January there's this bright band of them near the equator, right along the middle of the picture." Wyatt tapped the left image. "In July the band is way up over India and Bangladesh. Same band, different spot. I think." He frowned. "Or a different band that looks the same, which would ruin my whole argument."

Orion leaned in until his nose almost touched the paper. "Could you check with more pictures? Like, ones from spring?"

"That's exactly what I want to do." Wyatt raised his hand toward the reference desk, where Mr. Schneider was reshelving a cart of atlases. "Mr. Schneider, do you have satellite images from other months?"

Mr. Schneider tilted his head. "March? Let me see what the weather archives have. And I hope that granola bar stays outside the computers. Crumbs and keyboards have a serious allergy to each other." He disappeared into the stacks and came back with a thin binder of monthly images, smelling faintly of dust. "Evaluate them however you like, but the copier is the old one, so be patient with it."

Wyatt laid out March, May, and October in a row between his originals. Slowly he traced the cloudy stripe with one finger. March, a little above the equator. May, climbing. July, parked over South Asia like a lid. October, sliding back down.

"Okay," Orion said. "It moves. It's one thing moving. So what?"

"So, follow the sequence." Wyatt pulled his notebook over and sketched the band as a wobbly line in each month. "Every northern summer, that rainy band of rising air near the equator shifts north over South Asia. In July it's right on top of the rice fields. That's when the monsoon rains come." He tapped the sketch. "Farmers plant rice so the floods hit when the seedlings are ready for them. If the rains came in the wrong month, whole harvests would drown or dry out. That's why it matters."

"Does the band have a name, or are you going to call it 'the wobbly line' in your presentation?"

Wyatt flipped through the binder until he found the caption page. "Intertropical Convergence Zone," he read aloud. "That's the actual name. I'd better write it before I forget it."

Mr. Schneider drifted back over and looked at the row of images, then at Wyatt's sketch. "You tested it," he said quietly. "Multiple months, one pattern. That's more than most reports get." He straightened the binder's edge on the table. "Want me to fire up the copier for your July image? You'll want the big one for the class."

"Definitely the big one." Wyatt fed the page into the machine while Orion held the lid, and the two of them watched the light bar crawl beneath the glass, sweeping out a copy of South Asia wearing its summer clouds like a crown.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
story:
Arthur had been to the gurdwara every month since he was small, but tonight he had brought someone new. Camila followed him through the doors with her wallet already out, hunting for a price list or a donation jar with a fixed amount.

"Where do we pay?" she whispered as they took off their shoes.

"We don't," Arthur said.

"That can't be right." She looked around at the hall, where long rows of people sat cross-legged on the floor, waiting. "Nobody gives away food. My dad says there's always a catch."

Arthur remembered being six, standing in this same community hall, tugging his grandmother's sleeve and insisting that someone must have forgotten the cash box. She had laughed and made him watch the volunteers instead. He had counted them: men and women stirring enormous pots, ladling dal onto steel trays, moving down the rows. Nobody paid, and nobody charged. He'd finally decided the missing cash box wasn't missing at all. It just didn't exist.

"Watch," he told Camila now. "You'll see."

A volunteer set trays of food in front of each person, one after another, moving steadily down the line. Arthur pointed out an elderly man in a suit, a group of students in jeans, a woman who had just wandered in from the street. Camila's frown deepened, the way it did in science class when her hypothesis was about to collapse.

"So it really is free," she said slowly. "For everybody? Even people who aren't Sikh?"

"Every visitor," Arthur said. "It's called langar."

They sat down on the floor together with everyone else, and when the roti came around, still warm, Camila tore hers and stared at it like it was a prototype of some impossible machine. Arthur remembered his own turbulent first week at his new school, when he'd been sure he would never make a friend, and how Camila had been the one to sit with him anyway. He was glad he could hand something back.

Halfway through the meal, an aunty with flour on her sleeves paused beside them. "You two want to help with the roti?" she asked. "We can always use extra hands."

Camila glanced at Arthur. "Do we have to pay for that too?"

The aunty laughed so loudly that three people turned to look. "No, no. You give your time, that's all."

Behind the counter, Camila's first attempts were lopsided and pale, and the aunty showed her again how to press the dough flat. Her fourth one puffed up round and golden, and the aunty nodded. Arthur carried stacks of them out to the rows on the floor, placing them in front of strangers who smiled up at him.

On his last trip back, Camila pressed a fresh roti into his hands. "Eat," she said. "It's on the house."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
Michael had seventy-five cents in his pocket and a problem: the library's summer reading contest gave prizes to whoever recruited the most new members, and he wanted the telescope on the top shelf more than he had ever wanted anything. The sign above the sign-up table said JOIN THE WINNING TEAM, which made it sound like everyone was already doing it. Michael squinted at the sign. Was everyone doing it? He counted the names on the sign-up sheet. Eleven. Out of a whole town. Interesting.

He found Chiara at a table near the window, flipping through a magazine with a shiny ad on the back cover. A famous actor's face grinned out of it, holding a bottle of something green. "He drinks it every morning," Chiara read aloud, "so it must be good."

"Do you think he actually drinks it?" Michael asked. He leaned closer. The ad used words like "pure," "natural," and "healthy glow." He turned the page, looking for facts, and found only tiny print about prices. The big words felt warm and nice, but when he tried to figure out what they actually claimed, his fingers came up empty. They could mean almost anything. "It doesn't say what's in it," he said slowly. "It just says good-feeling stuff."

"Glittering generalities," said Paisley, dropping into the next chair with her stack of books. "That's what my brother calls them. Vague, positive words like 'freedom' or 'natural' that make you feel good without saying anything you can actually check." She popped a piece of gum in her mouth. "Ads are full of them."

Michael slid the magazine closer, testing the idea like a coin on a vending machine. "Healthy glow," he said. "Can I check that? Nope. Pure? Pure what?" Every glowing word, when he poked it, turned out to be made of air. Then he looked up at the library's own sign. JOIN THE WINNING TEAM. Winning, team. Warm words. Nothing checkable. He laughed out loud, and a kid at the next table shushed him.

"Your sign does the same thing," Chiara said, and he could hear the smile in her voice.

The consequence was inevitable: he tore the sign down and made a new one that said, "11 members. Help us reach 20. Free bookmarks on Fridays." Specific numbers, a real thing you could verify, and a promised bookmark. By closing time, three new names sat on the sheet. When Ms. Flores locked the doors, Michael stayed behind to console the boy who had wanted the telescope too and lost by two names, letting him hold it first under the porch light. "Look at the moon with it tomorrow," Michael said, pointing the lens up past the oak trees.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In France and many other European countries, prices use a comma where English uses a decimal point, so twelve euros fifty is written "12,50 €."
story:
Simon spread the printed menu across the kitchen table and smoothed out the creases. Ms. Smith had given it to him on Friday, a real menu from a café in Lyon, and on Monday he had to order from it entirely in French, out loud, in front of the whole class. He had practiced saying "Je voudrais un sandwich au jambon" until it came out smoothly, but the price line kept stopping him cold. The sandwich showed "6,50 €", the soup "4,25 €", and the steak frites read "12,50 €". He stared at that last number and felt something go brittle inside him, like the sound of a cracker breaking. Twelve hundred and fifty euros for a plate of steak and fries?

He called August, who had taken French last year. "There's a menu at my house," Simon said when he arrived, sliding it across the table. "Look at number twelve. The steak. How can anyone pay that much?"

August bent over the paper, frowning. He pulled out his phone and typed carefully, then typed again. "Wait. My aunt went to Paris and she said lunch was cheap there. Like ten euros." He turned the menu around so it faced Simon. "Every price has it. The soup is four hundred twenty-five euros? Nobody would sell soup for that."

Simon took the menu back and looked down the whole column, and a pattern began to surface. Every single price ended in two digits after the comma, never three, never one. Prices at home ended in two digits after a decimal point, like 12.50, meaning twelve fifty. He grabbed a pencil and wrote under the steak: 12,50 € is twelve euros fifty. Then he checked it against everything else. The soup at 4,25 would be four euros twenty-five. The sandwich at 6,50 would be six fifty. That made sense, ordinary café sense. "In France and a bunch of other European countries, they use a comma where we use a decimal point," he said. It wasn't a guess anymore; the whole menu proved it, the same way one cloud doesn't mean rain but a sky full of them does.

"So it's like a mirror," August said, tapping the comma and then the period Simon had written. "They write it backwards from us."

"Kind of." Simon thought about it. "The comma and the period coincide in the same spot on the number, doing the same job. There's a symmetry to it." He straightened the menu and stood up. "Okay. New plan. Order from me."

August cleared his throat. "Bonjour. Je voudrais le steak frites."

"Ça fait douze euros cinquante," Simon said, and the words came out steady.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
story:
Jorge's basement smelled like popcorn and old sneakers. The two of them had forty minutes before his mom drove them to swim practice, and the video game controller sat untouched between them because Ryan couldn't stop replaying Tuesday. At lunch, some kids in the next row had made fun of Lennon's stutter, copying it, laughing. Ryan had sat two seats away and said nothing. Neither had anyone else.

"You just watched?" Jorge asked, not looking up from tying his shoe.

"I froze. Okay? I didn't know what to say without making it worse." Ryan picked up the controller and put it down again. "If I'd yelled at them, they'd just come back harder at him. If I'd made a joke, it'd be a joke about Lennon anyway."

Jorge shrugged. "So do nothing forever?"

The question landed like a slap. Ryan thought about his older brother, who had once explained why soldiers check on civilians after a battle, not just during it. The after part mattered too. Maybe that was the piece he was missing. He kept hunting for some brave thing to do in the middle of a turbulent moment, when the whole problem might be in the quiet part afterward, where nobody was watching.

He grabbed his phone off the carpet and opened it, then closed it, then opened it again. "If I text Lennon now, is that weird?"

"It's weird if it's a paragraph. Just say what happened wasn't okay."

Ryan typed, deleted, typed. hey. what those guys did at lunch wasnt right. i shouldve said something. He stared at it. His thumb hovered over send while the game's title screen played its looping music, and the clock on the wall said they had thirty-one minutes left before practice.

He sent it.

The reply came fast, faster than he expected: thanks. thought i was the only one who noticed.

Then: you kinda learn whos real by who talks to you after.

Ryan read it twice. Nobody had stepped in on Tuesday, not him, not Jorge, not the kids who were usually decent. But apparently the silence afterward was the part that made Lennon feel alone, and a stupid three-line text had just cracked it. He could do that. He could always do that, even on the days he froze.

"Practice in twenty-five," Jorge said, standing and tossing Ryan his backpack.

Ryan caught it and, still holding the phone, typed one more message. wedesday. sit with us?

From the stairs, Jorge called down, "Tell him the respawn rule at lunch. He'll fit right in."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
The fight had started over a group project, when Chantelle told Hamza that Hazel had been "basically negligent" about her slides, and Hazel heard about it before lunch. Now Hazel sat on the low wall by the basketball court, squeezing a tennis ball so hard her wrist ached, somewhere near the tendon, she guessed, where the sting concentrated. Chantelle was across the playground pretending to study a fence.

Hazel turned the problem over the way she turned the ball. She was not angry anymore, exactly. The hot feeling had drained out during fourth period. But every time she imagined walking over and saying "we're friends again," something in her dug in its heels, and she wanted to know why. She tested it out loud, quietly, like a hypothesis. "Okay. I'm not mad. So why does 'best friends' feel too big?"

Hamza, who had been shooting free throws badly, wandered over. "Talking to yourself is a bad sign."

"Help me with something," Hazel said. "If you forgive someone, does that mean everything goes back to normal?"

He thought about it, bouncing the ball once. "My mom says no. She says forgiving and reconciling are different things. Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. She told me that when I was mad at my cousin last year."

"So you can do one without the other."

"I forgave him by Christmas," Hamza said. "We didn't rebuild anything till like, March. And it wasn't exactly the same friendship after. That part's allowed, apparently."

Hazel stood up. It felt like finding a rule for a game she'd been playing blind. She could let go of the resentment without promising the sleepovers and the shared locker and all of it, not yet, maybe not ever in the same shape. She crossed the playground, and Chantelle saw her coming and stopped pretending the fence was interesting.

"I forgive you," Hazel said. "For the negligent thing. Which, by the way, I did six slides."

"Five," Chantelle said. "But one of them was really good."

"I'm not saying we go back to how it was, though. Not today. My mom calls that reconciling, and it takes longer."

Chantelle considered this, then held out her fist, and Hazel bumped it. "Partial credit," Chantelle said. "Very you."

Ms. Rahimi, on yard duty, watched them from the door and gave a small nod, as if she'd been keeping score. Hamza's next free throw actually went in, which nobody could believe, and Chantelle yelled "witnessed!" so loudly that a seagull left the roof in a hurry.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
Alice stood outside the gym with her speech cards sweating in her hand, listening to the buzzer sound every thirty seconds. In four minutes she had to give her debate summary in front of the whole class, and her heart was hammering so hard she could feel it in her ears. Bree leaned against the wall beside her, chewing the end of her pencil.

"You look like you're about to pass out," Bree said.

"I'm not. It's just anxiety," Alice said. "My body thinks a class presentation is a bear attack." She tried to laugh, but it came out thin.

Inside the gym, Mr. Cardinal was running the soccer unit at the far end, and through the open door Alice watched the goalie, a girl from another class, crouch down in front of a penalty shot. The whole gym went quiet. Instead of freezing, the goalie let out one long, slow breath, so slow Alice could almost count it, and then settled into her stance. The shooter kicked, the goalie dove the right way, and the ball thumped into her gloves.

Alice stared. "Did you see that? She breathed out forever before the shot." Bree shrugged, but Alice's mind was already working. Maybe the long exhale wasn't just a habit. Maybe it was a coping skill, something you did on purpose before a stressful moment to calm the body's stress response. She had read those exact words on a poster in the counselor's hallway and thought they were decoration, but the goalie had used it like a tool. There was only one way to find out if it actually worked, and she had about two minutes to run the test on herself.

She pressed her back to the cool metal of the locker and breathed in through her nose, then let the air out slowly through her mouth, longer than the inhale, the way she remembered a coach describing to the goalie. "Slow breathing, long exhales," she muttered. "Fine, body. Let's see." Her chest still felt tight, but by the third breath the hammering had dropped to something she could think over. Her hands stopped shaking. It wasn't magic; it was more like turning the volume down.

"Alice, you're up," Mr. Cardinal called from the doorway, clipboard in hand.

She was still hesitant at the front of the room, and her first sentence came out wobbly. But she kept the slow exhales going between points, and by the time she reached her closing argument her voice was steady. Dalia caught her eye from the second row and gave a small thumbs up.

Afterward Mr. Cardinal read his critique aloud to the class, the way he did for everyone, and Alice braced herself to be humiliated. "Strongest closing so far," he said. "Shaky start, though. What happened?"

Alice glanced at Bree, who was grinning. "I figured something out in the hallway," Alice said. "Ask the goalie."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
story:
Alexander had been at camp for exactly one day, and he already knew three things: the lake was freezing, the counselor's whistle was loud, and his buddy was a kid named Calvin who talked with his whole face. They had been paired at the waterfront that morning, which meant, as Calvin explained cheerfully, "We're a buddy pair, so at a buddy check you have to find me fast and hold up your hand." Alexander had nodded, but he'd been busy watching a heron stalk the reeds at the far end of the beach, and he hadn't really listened.

After lunch there was free swim again. Alexander put on his suit, waited for the whistle, and then slipped back to the cabin to grab the crumpled letter his mom had tucked into his duffel. He read it twice, found a granola bar in his pocket, and came back down the hill eating it, feeling pleased with himself. That was when he heard the whistle blast three times, short and sharp, and saw the whole beach erupt. Swimmers scrambled out of the water in pairs, arms shooting up, fingers raised in twos.

Staff moved along the shoreline counting heads. Alexander spotted Calvin standing alone in the shallows, scanning the sand with a face gone pale and tight. "Where were you?" Calvin shouted the moment he saw him. "At a buddy check we have to find each other quick so they can count everyone, and I couldn't find you anywhere. They were about to clear the whole lake."

Alexander raised his hand, fingers up in a two, and Calvin slammed his own hand against it like they'd won something. A counselor jogged over, counted them, and moved on, though he gave Alexander a long look. "I was in the cabin," Alexander confessed, quieter than he meant to. "I didn't think it mattered if I wasn't swimming."

"That's the thing," Calvin said. "I'm your buddy whether you swim or not. Every camper at the waterfront is paired with a partner. You could've been the strongest swimmer here and it wouldn't be equivalent to being counted. Nobody's counted without their buddy." Mr. Sandhu, the waterfront director, waved them toward the towel rack and told the group that anyone who left the beach had to sign out with a buddy or a counselor, so no one would ever be a missing-person candidate by accident.

Alexander promised to sign out next time. He even meant it. Then, on the way back up the hill, Calvin stopped dead beside the waterfront shack, squinting at the sign-out sheet clipped to the board. At the top of the page, in someone's careful printing, was the day's first entry: Calvin's own name, signed out to the nurse's cabin at nine that morning, and never signed back in. "I forgot I did that," Calvin said weakly. "I made them search the lake for me."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Mandarin Chinese, "Duōshǎo qián?" means "How much money?" and is the everyday way to ask a price.
story:
Alexandra spread her flashcards across the library table so fast that two slid off the edge and landed face down, which felt like a bad omen. On Saturday her family was going to Grand Harbor, a real Chinese restaurant, and she had promised her grandmother she would order the dumplings herself, in Mandarin, without pointing at the menu like a lost tourist. The problem was that she could say "I want dumplings" but had no idea how to ask the price, and if the total came to more money than she had, she would be standing there with her wallet open like a jar of dust.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Patience, dropping into the next chair with her own homework.

"I'm defusing embarrassment," Alexandra said. "Which is worse."

Jeff leaned over from the other side and picked up a card. He read it out in a pronunciation so terrible that Ms. Wanjiru, shelving books two aisles away, made a small sound like a kettle deciding not to whistle. "That contradicts everything on the card," Alexandra told him. "You just said 'I would like a small haircut of soup.'"

"Sounds delicious," Jeff said, and Patience snorted into her sleeve.

Alexandra flipped through the cards again. Every card had a word, a meaning, and a small drawing, because she learned better with drawings. There was the card for dumplings, with a fat little moon of a dumpling on it. There was the card for rice, with a bowl. There was the card for tea, with a cup so stained-looking that she suspected the previous owner had actually used it as a coaster. The corners of the cards were soft and frayed, the lamination gone at the edges; the erosion of careful thumbing by every student who had checked out this set before her. She found that oddly encouraging. Other people had needed this too.

Then she found a card at the back that someone had written by hand, in pencil, in looping letters: "Duōshǎo qián? It means How much money? Say it like: dwaw-shao chyen. Trust me, this is the everyday way to ask a price. Signed, a survivor of the Grand Harbor line." Alexandra read it three times. Whoever the survivor was, they had faced the exact dragon she was facing, and they had left behind the sword.

She tested it immediately, because a card could lie. "Patience, ask me how much something costs, any language."

"How much is this sandwich?"

"Duōshǎo qián?" Alexandra said, and Jeff gasped like she had pulled a rabbit from her ear.

At lunch she took her practice to the cafeteria line, which she declared to be a restaurant, and Patience played cashier with a milk crate as the register. Jeff ordered in his haircut-of-soup voice and was charged one imaginary million dollars. When Alexandra reached the front, she asked, "Duōshǎo qián?" and Patience, deadpan, said, "Six dollars," and Alexandra counted out six grapes, and the whole line applauded, which for a cafeteria meant three people clapped while the rest stared.

On Saturday, Grand Harbor smelled of star anise and steam. The fish tank near the register glowed luminous green, and the dumpling stall behind it was crowded. Alexandra joined the line, and while she waited she said the question under her breath, over and over, her lips moving like a tiny engine. When she reached the front, the woman in the tall white hat raised her eyebrows. Alexandra pointed at the dumplings and said, clear and whole, "Duōshǎo qián?" The woman smiled and held up eight fingers, and Alexandra paid before her brain could panic. Walking back to the table with the steaming box, she caught her grandmother's eye and grinned.

"Duōshǎo qián?" her grandmother asked, nodding at the box.

"For you, free," Alexandra said, and set it down in the middle of the table.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
story:
Abigail spread her poster board across the bleacher seats at the far end of the gymnasium, where the science fair tables were already marked with tape. Her title read, in tall blue letters, "Music Is Good for Plants." Yasmin plopped down beside her with two granola bars and handed one over without being asked, because she knew Abigail forgot to eat when she was working.

"That's your whole project?" Yasmin said, chewing. "Four words?"

"It's a hypothesis," Abigail said. "Ms. Mori told us a useful hypothesis has to be testable. That means an experiment could actually show it's wrong. Like a prediction. You're supposed to write it 'If... then...'"

"So write it that way."

Abigail stared at the poster. If music is good for plants, then what? She tried, "If music is good for plants, then a plant near music will grow taller than one without music." Saying it out loud made something click. Good was a feeling word. Taller was a number she could measure and maybe be wrong about. She grabbed the marker and crossed out the old title, then wrote the new sentence along the bottom edge of the board, her handwriting getting smaller as she ran out of room.

Yasmin leaned over to clarify one thing. "Taller than what, though?"

"Than a plant with no music. Same pot, same window, same water. Everything the same except the music." Eliana arrived with her own project, a baking soda volcano trailing a smell of vinegar, and asked what they were doing. Abigail explained, and Eliana frowned.

"But what if they grow the same? Then you're wrong in front of everybody."

"Then I'm wrong in front of everybody," Abigail said. "That's kind of the point. If nothing could prove me wrong, it's not really an experiment."

Eliana considered this while adjusting her volcano's paper cone. "That's actually the most systematic thing I've ever heard you say. Usually you lose your shoes twice a day."

Abigail's older cousin had offered to tutor her in science after midterm grades came out, and honestly the sessions were starting to feel worth the Saturday mornings. She checked her seedlings, three in pots lined up in a shoebox by the gym door, all of them a stubborn two centimeters tall so far, music or no music. Two weeks until the fair. Plenty of time to be right, or to be interestingly wrong.

Ms. Mori walked past, glanced at the rewritten sentence, and gave a small nod. Abigail uncapped the marker again and added a column to her data table labeled "no music, control," while Yasmin held the poster steady against the breeze from the propped-open door.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
story:
Isaac's fingers kept tripping over the same four measures in the garage, where the old upright piano lived between the lawnmower and a shelf of paint cans. Daven sat on an overturned bucket, wincing every time Isaac flubbed the passage. "You've played it like forty times," Daven said. "It's not getting better. It might be getting worse."

Isaac stopped and stared at his hands. That was the strange part. He wasn't speeding up or looking at the wrong keys, yet the sequence fell apart at the same spot every single time, like something hidden was sabotaging him. He tried it once more, slowly, and even at half speed his thumb landed wrong. "Okay," he said, closing the lid. "I quit for today."

He slept badly anyway, worrying about the recital, and in the morning he wandered out to the garage in his pajamas to look at the sheet music one more time. He wasn't going to practice; he just wanted to see the notes. But his hands were already moving, and the tricky passage came out clean, fast, and easy, as if the mistakes had gone dormant overnight. Isaac played it again, then a third time, laughing out loud. He hadn't practiced once since yesterday, and somehow he was better.

He asked Ms. Mansour about it when she came over to borrow the ladder. "Yesterday I couldn't play it at all," he said, "and today I can, without any extra practice. Is that a thing, or am I imagining it?" She nodded. "It's a real thing. Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve your performance the next day, no extra practice needed." Isaac felt a jolt of curiosity. "So sleep is like secret practice?" "Sleep after practicing, yes. That's what the studies found." She carried the ladder to her yard, and Isaac stood there wondering how many other things his brain was working on without telling him.

He decided to test it. That evening he drilled a different passage, one he'd never managed cleanly, until it was a mess, then forced himself to stop and go to bed. The next morning he marched to the garage with Daven, who had agreed to be a witness. Isaac took a breath, put his fingers on the keys, and played. The notes locked together, measure after measure, all the way to the end.

"Okay," Daven said slowly, "we need an alliance. You teach my hands to do that, and I'll bring the snacks."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
