knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
Nolan leaned against the gym door at 7:02 in the morning, his fingers cold around his phone, his breath fogging in the empty hallway. The school's fall festival would sell exactly two hundred wristbands at two dollars each, and last year they had sold out before second period. When the online store opened at 7:05, he tapped refresh, tapped again, and watched the little spinning wheel spin and spin until the page went gray. Sold out. Three minutes.

In homeroom, Korbin slid into the next seat and dropped his own phone on the desk like it had betrayed him. "I was in by 7:06," he said. "Nothing. Pierre got one, though." Across the room Pierre held up his wrist, where the orange band already glowed under the fluorescent lights. He had woken up at six, waiting by the door of the virtual store like it was a real line.

Nolan couldn't stop turning it over. Two hundred bands, and it seemed like half the school wanted one. He remembered the pizza fundraiser in spring, when the booster club had sold slices for a dollar and the trays were empty by noon while a crowd stood around grumbling, hungry. Mr. Nur had handed him the last slice that day, saying only, "Demand has teeth today." Nolan hadn't understood then. Now something clicked, quiet and sure, the way a key turns.

At lunch he found Pierre by the vending machines, where the smell of burnt popcorn hung in the air. "Ask me why the bands vanished," Nolan said. Pierre raised an eyebrow. Nolan laid it out. "Two dollars is too low. At that price, way more people want a band than there are bands. There's a gap between how many people want them and how many exist, and that gap has a name. It's called a shortage." Pierre chewed that over, then said the word slowly, testing it. "A shortage. Huh. So the price is the problem, not the website."

"So test it," Nolan said, and his voice came out lower than he meant it to. "Tomorrow the student store sells the leftover autumn keychains. Fifty of them, three dollars each, and nobody's been talking about them. If I'm right about the rule, plenty should still be there at lunch." Pierre shook his hand on it, solemn as a treaty, and Korbin demanded in.

The next day the hallway outside the store smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings. Nolan walked in slowly, his heart ticking, and there they were: rows of little bronze-colored alloy keychains, the school's ram stamped into each one, more than forty still hanging on the rack at 12:30. He bought one, the metal cool and heavier than he expected in his palm, and turned it over twice.

Korbin arrived breathless, staring at the full rack, then at Nolan. "So if they'd priced the wristbands higher," Korbin said, "some of us wouldn't have gotten shut out, and some of us wouldn't have bought at all." Nolan nodded, clipped the keychain to his backpack zipper, and heard the tiny click.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A strong thesis makes a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with; a statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue.
story:
Maria had been dreading Monday's writing club all weekend, because Ms. Wardak had promised that on Monday everyone would hand in a thesis statement and a three-point outline before drafting a single paragraph. Now she sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a bowl of pistachios, a laptop, and a blank document titled "Essay Outline" that had been blank for forty minutes.

Her grandmother slid a cup of tea across the table and looked at the screen. "When I was a girl, we argued about everything at this table," she said. "Your grandfather still argues with the radio. Try a topic you could argue with him about."

Maria typed: School should start later. Then she frowned. She remembered Tea reading her own thesis aloud at the last club meeting: "Pollution is bad for the environment." Lana had burst out laughing, and Maria had laughed too, though she hadn't known why it was funny until Ms. Wardak asked the room, "Who here disagrees? Anyone? Can you argue against it?" Nobody could, because it was just true, the way "rain is wet" is true. Ms. Wardak had said, "A strong thesis makes a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with. A statement nobody would dispute gives an essay nothing to argue." Tea had rewritten hers three times that day.

So Maria tested her own sentence. She imagined her grandfather across the table, waving a pistachio at her. "School should start later." Would he argue? He would. He would say his father woke at four to milk goats and walked six kilometers to school. That was a real disagreement, not just stubbornness. She wrote her three points underneath: teenagers sleep differently than adults, grades improve in schools with later starts, and attendance goes up. Then she checked each point against the thesis, the way her grandmother checked a vessel of rice water for salt, tasting before adding more.

Her grandmother leaned over, reading. "Attendance goes up? Prove it."

"That's the whole point," Maria said. "I have to prove all of it, because you could disagree."

"I could," her grandmother said. "I think mornings build character. Character is not subjective, unlike your opinion about sleeping."

Maria laughed and typed a fourth point, then cut it, because three points was the assignment. She spent another twenty minutes sharpening the thesis wording, since "later" could mean ten minutes or two hours, and she could already hear her grandfather asking which.

On Monday, Tea slid into the seat beside her before the bell. "Tell me yours is arguable," Tea whispered. "Ms. Wardak rejected my new one. She said everyone agrees the library should have more books."

Maria read her thesis off the page, and Tea immediately said, "Wrong, mornings are better, you love mornings, you told me."

"Then it's a good thesis," Maria said, and clicked print.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Kate raised her hand before Ms. Costa had even finished handing out the papers. "If both sides wrote down what happened, why can't we just read them and know?"

Ms. Costa set a photocopy on Kate's desk. "Read them tonight and tell me."

The history club met on Thursdays in the back of the library, and Kate had come armed. She slapped the two pages on the table in front of Reet and Breanna. "Okay. Here's a colonial witness from that morning at Lexington in April 1775. He says the British fired first." She tapped the second sheet. "And here's a British witness. He says the colonists fired first."

"They can't both be right," Breanna said.

"Obviously." Reet leaned over the pages. "So one of them is lying."

Kate had spent half the night on that idea, and it kept falling apart. "Lying about what? Nobody knew who fired the first shot would end up in every textbook in the country. They were just standing there in the dark and the smoke. Whoever fired it, half the people on that field probably never even saw it happen." She paused, assessing her own argument. "So maybe nobody's lying. Maybe they're both just... wrong."

Breanna frowned. "Both wrong about the same single shot?"

"Both sure," Kate said. "That's worse."

Ms. Costa drifted over from the shelves, but she only listened, arms folded, which was her way of making them do the work. Reet picked up the colonial account and read it aloud, then the British one, and the rest of the club argued about which witness seemed more credible. The British soldier wrote calmly, with details about the weather. The colonial witness sounded angry and certain. Half the club decided the calm one was telling the truth.

"That's not evidence," Kate said. "That's style." She stood up and went to the whiteboard and drew a Venn diagram, one circle for each side. "Everything they agree on goes in the middle. They agree on the date, the place, that a shot started everything. The contradiction is only about who fired it." She stepped back. "If two people saw the same morning and got the same things right, then the disagreement isn't about lying or truth. It's about where they were standing."

"So historians just... don't know?" Breanna said.

"Historians still don't know," Kate said. "Nobody ever found out who fired that first shot. Two hundred and fifty years, and it's still open."

The room went quiet. Reet looked almost deflated, like a mystery without an ending had cheated her somehow. "Then what was the point of reading them?"

Kate wanted to say something about how knowing the limits of knowing was itself worth something, but that sounded like a poster. Instead she erased her diagram, leaving the two circles blank, and wrote one word between them: "Unknown."

"Every other question in this book has an answer in the back," she said. "This one we get to keep."

Reet copied the empty circles into her notebook, which for Reet was practically an apology, and Breanna said, "So whoever fired that shot got the whole war started and nobody ever even wrote down his name."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older, in 1669.
story:
Avery dumped the last bucket of sand behind the fence and stared at the lumpy hill she had built in the corner of the backyard. Tomorrow she had to explain to her class how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and all she had so far was a pile of dirt and a garden hose. Her first attempt had gone badly. When she poured water over the top, the whole mound collapsed sideways into a flat gray pancake.

"You buried my shoe," Quinten said, digging his sneaker out of the pancake. "Again."

"It's supposed to make a canyon, not a beach," Avery said. Veronica sat cross-legged on the grass, turning the hose nozzle over in her hands like it might confess a secret.

"The water keeps winning," Veronica said. "It just demolishes everything at once."

Avery sat back on her heels and thought about that. A real canyon did not get demolished at once. It got carved slowly, and the river kept flowing in the same place, day after day, year after year, while the dirt and pebbles it picked up got carried off and dropped somewhere downstream. The problem wasn't the water. The problem was that her hill had no layers. It was one soft blob from top to bottom, so nothing could hold its shape while the water cut through.

"We need strata," she said. "Layers. Like a cake." She remembered the museum trip in October, standing in front of the wall of striped rock with Veronica and Quinten while Mr. Foster, their neighbor, had pointed at a sign. The sign said that in 1669, the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older. She hadn't thought much about it then, but now she grabbed her backpack and dug out the crumpled pamphlet from the trip.

"Listen," she said. "'In 1669, the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older.' So if we build our hill in layers, the bottom one is like the oldest rock. The water will cut down through them, and you'll be able to see the whole history."

"It's like reading pages," Veronica said. "Bottom of the stack, oldest page."

They rebuilt the hill all afternoon. Avery mixed sand with a little clay, then packed in a layer of pebbles, then more sand, then a band of dark coffee grounds Mr. Foster donated over the fence from his compost bin. "Nicolas Steno," he said, watching them work. "That man caused a revolution in how people read rocks." He went back to trimming his hedge, and Avery pressed each layer down with the flat of the trowel until the hill looked like a striped loaf of bread standing knee-high in the grass.

Quinten turned the hose on low and held it steady at one spot on the slope. The water darkened the top layer, found a seam, and began to run. It didn't collapse this time. A narrow channel sank between the pebble layer and the sand, widened, dropped a small fan of sediment at the base, and kept cutting. When they bent close, they could count the layers exposed in the tiny cliff wall: light, dark, dotted with pebbles, light again, all the way down.

"Look at the walls," Veronica said. "You can see every layer it cut through."

"Vigorous flow, deep canyon," Quinten said, and opened the nozzle a quarter turn. The water surged, and a whole slab of the oldest layer slumped into the stream. Avery laughed and reached for the camera on the picnic table.

"Perfect," she said. "That's slide four."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Florence lined up five clay beads on the kitchen table and touched each one, one at a time, with the back of her knuckle. They felt cool, all of them, and cool meant damp, and damp meant danger. She had learned that the hard way on Tuesday, when Ms. Fortin lifted her bowl out of the kiln line and set it on a shelf by itself. "This one's still wet inside," Ms. Fortin had said, and moved on to Deborah's plate. Deborah's plate went into the kiln. Florence's bowl did not. The whole class had watched, and Florence had felt the heat of humiliation crawl up her neck, worse because she couldn't argue. The bowl had looked dry. It had felt dry on the outside. Something she couldn't see had given it away.

She poured herself some water and thought about that. Ms. Fortin hadn't cut the bowl open or weighed it. She had known anyway. Florence picked up a bead and held it against her cheek, the way her mother tested a baby bottle. The bead was colder than her skin. That, she decided, was the clue. Water made clay cool, even when the surface looked dusty and finished. So the rule had to be simple: if it feels cooler than me, there's still water hiding in there, and water trapped in clay turns to steam in the kiln and can crack or burst the whole thing apart.

Just to be sure, she tried an experiment. She dampened one corner of a paper towel and pressed it against her wrist, then pressed a dry corner against the other wrist. The wet side felt colder instantly. Same wrist, same moment. She sat back, satisfied. The beads weren't dry yet, even though they looked it, and she wasn't going to guess again.

The phone buzzed on the table. Aminata had sent a picture of her coil pot with the message, "Totally dry, firing tomorrow, jealous of your beads?" Florence typed back, "Mine aren't dry. Holding them a week." She hesitated, because she had planned to rush. She'd wanted her beads fired in the same batch as everyone else's work, ready for the art show on Friday. Now she was giving that up. She adjusted her plan in her head: beads for the spring show instead, and the art room's display shelf could have her bowl, which had finally gone into the kiln yesterday.

Aminata replied with a single question mark, and Florence typed, "Wet clay explodes in the kiln. Steam. Look it up if you don't believe me."

After a minute the answer came back: "Oh. Good call. Mine is going in the window to dry longer."

Florence grinned, slid the beads to the sunniest spot on the table, right where the afternoon light came through, and turned the brightest one so its whole face caught the warmth.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Charlie sat in the back seat of the family car with her shoes off and her dance ticket folded into four in her pocket. Maliyah was already at the gym, and Yousuf was meeting them at the door. Her dad drove with the radio off, which meant he wanted to talk.

"So this is your first one," he said. "Your cousin went to about twenty of these. Total veteran."

"I'm going for the snacks," Charlie said. "And to see if it's as bad as everyone says."

The gym had been decorated with paper streamers and a balloon arch that listed to one side, as if it had tried to eliminate itself from the evening early. Mr. Clarke-Williams stood at the door taking tickets. Inside, the music came from two giant speakers stacked on the stage, and the floor near them was empty in a perfect rectangle, like the whole school already knew something Charlie didn't.

Yousuf was standing in that empty space anyway, near the speakers, doing a sort of stiff marching step. Maliyah joined him. Charlie walked over, and after two songs her ears began to feel strange, a fuzzy pressure that stayed even between songs. Maliyah shouted something Charlie couldn't make out. Yousuf shouted it again, and she caught the word "weird."

They backed away to the folding tables by the wall. "It's better here," Maliyah said, working her jaw.

Charlie got a napkin and wrote on it: 85 decibels is safe for 8 hours. She'd read it on a poster in the library, next to a warning about lawn mowers. She underlined it. "Some U.S. agency called NIOSH," she said. "That's the limit they say."

"So we're fine," Yousuf said. "We've been here forty minutes."

"No, wait." Charlie flipped the napkin over. "The poster said every 3 more decibels halves it. So if the speakers are doing 88, that's four hours. At 91 it's two." She looked at the empty rectangle by the stage. "The 3-decibel rule is the trick. It doesn't go up slow."

Yousuf held his phone up like a microphone. "There's an app for this." He squinted at it. "It says about 90 by the speakers. Here it says 82."

"Then here is fine," Charlie said. "Near the stage, you'd want to leave by intermission."

"The probable best idea," Maliyah said, "is the snack table, all night, forever."

They stayed by the wall through the slow songs and the limbo contest, which Yousuf won by simply being the shortest. When the DJ turned the volume up for the last song, Charlie watched a group of kids move backward from the stage in a slow tide, one girl covering her ears. She checked Yousuf's phone again: 95 near the speakers. She did the napkin math in her head, twice, because the answer seemed too short.

A boy from her math class tapped her shoulder and pointed at the empty rectangle. "Why does nobody stand there? Best spot in the gym."

"Science," Charlie said.

He looked at the speakers, then at her napkin. "Can I see that?"

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
Grace had waited all summer for her cousin's old phone, and now it sat in her pocket, dead, before lunch on the very first day of school. At her locker she held down the power button and got nothing but a dark screen, which meant she had missed the photos Leona sent of the science room's new terrarium, humid and green behind the glass, with a label that read Herbivore Insects Only.

"It died again," Grace said at the lunch table. "I charged it all night. The bar said full."

Leona leaned over to look. "That happened to my brother's old phone. It would say full and then just quit." She scrolled back through the group chat, which was mostly their families trading reminders about pickups and practice, and found a message from Gus's mom: Does anyone know why old phones lose their battery so fast?

Gus dropped his tray onto the table. "My dad says they're lithium-ion," he said. "As they age, they hold less charge, so the battery life just keeps getting shorter." He shrugged like it was bad news and also just a fact of life.

Grace turned that over while she ate. So the phone wasn't lying when it said full. The battery itself was smaller now, in a way you couldn't see, like a jug that looked the same but secretly held less. Full was no longer really full. She couldn't fix that, but maybe she could work around it, if she could see the pattern clearly. After school she sat at the kitchen counter and drew a chart on graph paper to illustrate her idea: she would write down the charge every hour and mark exactly when the phone quit. Day one, it died at 11:40. Day two, 11:55. Day three, 11:38.

"There's my engineer," said her father, glancing at the chart on his way to the fridge.

"It dies around the same time every day," Grace said. "So it's the battery, not something I'm doing." She typed a message into the family group chat: Can someone remind me to plug in my phone at morning break? Her mother replied with a thumbs up before the screen went dark again.

On Thursday, Grace plugged the phone into the library outlet at 10:30, and at lunch the screen still glowed when Leona sent the terrarium pictures. A fat green caterpillar was munching a milkweed leaf, and the caption read: officially our herbivore. Grace took a screenshot, then checked the battery bar, which sat stubbornly at half, its edges soft and unreliable now that she knew what full really meant. She opened the group chat and typed: it survived the whole day. Then she added, day one of many, and pressed send.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them.
story:
The gym smelled like vinegar and burned popcorn, which meant the science fair was officially underway. Connor stood beside his project, a hand-drawn periodic table, and glared at the two empty boxes he had accidentally created by skipping from element 30 straight to 32. Dorothy leaned over his shoulder with the predatory grin of someone who had spotted a weakness.

"Your table is missing something," she said, tapping the gap. "Element 31 just doesn't exist in your universe. Congratulations, you've destroyed an element."

Before Connor could defend himself, Ms. Sharma intervened, kneeling to study the poster. "You know, the man who built the first periodic table left empty spaces on purpose. Mendeleev left gaps for elements that had not been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them." She straightened up. "So the question is, was your gap on purpose?"

Connor said yes, of course, with total confidence, and then panicked quietly once she walked away. Gallium. He pulled out his chem textbook and found gallium sitting at atomic number 31, right in his blank box. Then he noticed something that made his stomach do a small flip: the big number in each square, the atomic number, matched a smaller fact he'd half remembered. He counted carefully. Hydrogen, atomic number 1, had 1 proton. Carbon, 6, had 6 protons. Gallium, 31, had 31 protons. "The atomic number is the number of protons," he said out loud, accidentally, and a passing kindergartner gave him a strange look.

"It's also the number of times you've said that," said Nash, who had wandered over from his volcano project. Nash's volcano had erupted twelve times already and he was deeply jealous of anything with a working display. "My median eruption height is eight centimeters, in case anyone's asking. Nobody is, but still."

"That's actually cool," Connor said. "But look, if I put gallium back in, the whole pattern holds. Thirty-one protons, right where the gap was." He grabbed a marker, wrote GA and 31 in the empty box, and drew a little crown on it. "King of the gap."

Dorothy folded her arms. "Fine. I change my mind. It's the best poster here, and I only say that because Nash's volcano just ate a judge's clipboard." Across the gym, foam was bubbling onto a very patient man's shoes.

Nash sprinted toward the baking soda. "We had a deal, big guy!"

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
Aaron sent the message to the family group chat at 7:04 on Friday night: "Dance starts at 8. What do I wear." His mom replied with a photo of a shirt she had apparently been holding ready since Tuesday. His dad sent a thumbs up and then, thirty seconds later, a video of himself doing a dance move from 1998. Aaron typed "please never do that again" and put the phone in his pocket, because Kody was already knocking on the door.

The gym had been transformed into something with a fog machine and a wall of lights, and Mr. McKenzie, who taught science by day, was running the DJ booth like a man taking revenge on silence. Kody headed straight for the speakers, because Kody's whole plan for the night was to stand in what he called "the speaker zone" and become, in his words, "a legend." Giuliana came with them partway, but she kept glancing back at the photo booth, where she was trying to get a picture of the entire seventh grade doing the same pose for the yearbook page she had somehow gotten herself put in charge of.

Aaron stood next to Kody in the speaker zone for four songs. During the fifth one, he noticed a thin whistle in his ears that did not go away when the song ended. He pressed his palms against them, then let go. Still there, like a mosquito that had moved in permanently. His phone buzzed against his leg: the family group chat. Grandma had written, "TURN IT UP I LOVE THIS ONE," followed by, "At my age you need a strong constitution for these speakers, thank goodness mine is strong." His dad had replied, "My dance moves have been dormant since 1998 but tonight they have AWOKEN." Aaron exhaled slowly through his nose, put the phone away, and tapped Kody on the shoulder. "Do your ears whistle?" Kody yelled, "WHAT," from a foot away, which was its own answer.

The next morning the whistle was still there, quieter but stubborn, like it had signed a lease. Aaron sat at the kitchen counter with cereal and his phone, typing carefully: ears ringing after loud music. He read the screen twice, then a third time, because it said something he had never heard before. Then he opened the family chat and, after some thought, the three-way chat with Kody and Giuliana.

"Hey," he wrote. "The ringing thing has a name. It's called tinnitus." He sent the rest of what he had read: ringing after loud music is a warning sign that your ears got noise loud enough to damage hearing. Kody replied with eight crying faces and the words "MY LEGEND EARS." Giuliana wrote, "This is why I stayed by the photo booth," and attached the yearbook picture, in which Kody, mid-yell near the speakers, had his eyes closed in every single shot.

There was another dance in three weeks, and Aaron had a plan, which was less of a plan and more of a distance. He and Kody would stand by the water table, a solid twenty feet from Mr. McKenzie, and Aaron had texted Giuliana to confirm the spot was in range of the photo booth. On the night of the second dance, they took their positions. Mr. McKenzie dropped the beat, the fog machine coughed, and Kody leaned over the water table and shouted, "If we can still hear each other, we're doing it wrong." "No," Aaron shouted back. "If we can still hear each other, we're doing it exactly right." He stood there through six songs, and when the lights came up, his ears were quiet. Grandma's message arrived before he even reached his jacket: "GOOD SONG SELECTION. MY CONSTITUTION HOLDS."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and old magazines, and Sadie sat with her hands folded while the fluorescent light buzzed overhead. She had come to dread these appointments ever since the stomachaches started, and today she dreaded one thing above all: that the doctor would find nothing again, and her mother would give her that look. The last time, a nurse had slid a translucent plastic cup across the counter and asked for a sample, and the results had come back perfect, which somehow felt worse than being sick.

In the waiting room a poster hung crooked beside the window, the same one from Mr. Li's health class. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, it said, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Sadie had copied those words into her notebook three weeks ago without thinking much of them, but now she stared at the word social until the letters went strange. Her stomach had started hurting right after she and Noelle stopped talking, which was after Noelle told Selah something Sadie had asked her to keep private. Maybe the ache was not from anything you could see in a cup.

"Sadie," the nurse called, and the scale in the hallway announced her weight in big gray numbers. The doctor pressed on her belly, asked about sleep and food, and said everything felt normal. "One more question," she said, tapping her pen. "How are things going at school? With friends?" Sadie felt her face heat up. "Fine," she said, but her stomach twisted at the word, right there on the table, like it was answering for her.

That night she decided to test it, the way Mr. Li had shown them with the bean plants in seventh grade: change one thing and watch. If the social part really counted, then fixing a friendship might fix something else too. She texted Noelle and asked if they could talk before first period. Noelle answered at 10:42: ok. Just ok, which could mean anything.

They stood by the gym doors in the cold while buses groaned into the lot. "You told Selah what I said about my dad," Sadie began, and Noelle looked at her shoes and admitted it. "I panicked. I'm sorry." Sadie had spent weeks somewhere near despair about it, telling herself the friendship was over, but standing here she understood she could set a boundary instead of a wall. "I need you to not do that," she said. "Even if you panic. That's the deal." Noelle nodded, her breath a small white cloud. "Deal," she said, and pulled two gloves from her pocket, offering one. Sadie took it. Her stomach, she noticed, had gone quiet, and the bell was still a full minute away.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
Isabella pushed her pasta around the plate while her phone buzzed for the third time. Zack had sent another screenshot: the glitter sneakers, the ones Lilou had worn to the spring dance, now selling online for two hundred dollars. The retail price had been forty. She had the forty. She did not have the two hundred.

"Put the phone away at the table," her dad said, which she did, and which changed nothing about the sneakers.

She told him about them anyway, because a problem shared is a problem someone else has to listen to. "Everybody wants them now," she said. "There were only a few thousand pairs made. Lilou got hers before anyone cared."

Her dad grunted in a way that meant he was thinking. "You know what I saw at Mr. Kelly's garage sale last weekend? He had a box of old comic books, a whole stack of the same issue. He started them at five dollars each and nobody touched them. By noon he was down to a dollar and they went, every last one."

"That's just selling out," Isabella said.

"Same thing happened in reverse with his old canoe," her dad went on. "One canoe, and three different guys came by wanting it. He kept raising the price until exactly one of them still wanted it. One canoe, one buyer, and it sold." He speared a meatball. "He kept saying some economics word while he did it."

"What word?"

Her dad shrugged. "Equilibrium price, I think. Or market-clearing price, something like that."

Isabella chewed on that along with her pasta. The fad had colonized the entire eighth grade by now; glitter sneakers were all anyone talked about during what used to be leisure time at lunch. Two hundred dollars was what two hundred people would pay. But glitter went out of style fast, and fickle people were, in their own way, a kind of supply.

After dinner she texted Zack and Lilou. Wait two weeks, she typed. When everyone who has to have them already has them, and the sellers still have pairs left, the price drops until the pairs left equal the buyers left. She remembered Mr. Kelly's comic box. The stack cleared at a dollar because a dollar was where wanting met having.

Two and a half weeks later, right on schedule, the listing in her feed read sixty dollars. She checked the seller's page twice to make sure the shoes were authentic, counted her birthday money, and pressed Buy.

"Got them," she texted Zack.

He sent back a single crying emoji and a screenshot of his own order, placed that morning, at one hundred and ninety.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Mr. Tehrani had prescribed exactly one primary source for the project, and by Tuesday afternoon Mathis still hadn't opened it. Now he sat at the corner table of the public library with the scanned pages of an 1847 settler's diary in front of him, wishing the dead man had written anything other than "we departed the farm on the 9th" in handwriting like fence wire.

Arno dropped into the chair across from him with two granola bars and slid one across the table, because he knew Mathis forgot to eat when he was stuck. "That's the diary? It's tiny."

"It's three months of a family leaving Missouri," Mathis said. "I have to explain why people moved west in the 1800s using only this. Not a textbook. Just him."

Loralie arrived still out of breath from the rain outside, hair dripping, and Mathis got up without a word and brought her a handful of paper towels from the desk by the copier. She wiped her sleeves and leaned over the pages. "Start where it gets interesting."

They read aloud in turns, taking the parts of the settler, his wife, and the entries themselves. The crop had failed twice. The father's debt was written in ink with the amount underlined. Then, further in: letters from a cousin in Oregon describing free land, rivers full of fish, a town already building a school. Arno tapped the table.

"So they left because of the debt," he said, "but also because of the free land. Two different reasons."

"Kind of opposite reasons," Loralie said. "One shoves you out the door. The other one's out there waving you over."

Mathis sat back. "Mr. Tehrani kept saying push factors and pull factors in class. I thought it was just vocabulary." He copied two columns in his notebook. Under push he listed the failed crops and the debt, driving the family away from home. Under pull he listed the free land and the rivers, attracting them to a new place. Then he found the entry about the wife's brother, who had gone west the year before "of his own voluntary wish," and added him to the pull column, since a known face pulled as hard as any promise.

"The teacher wanted one source," Arno said, reading the notebook upside down. "You've got a whole system out of it."

From the front desk, Mr. Tehrani happened to be returning a biography of Andrew Jackson, and he paused behind them just long enough to see the two columns. "Perfect," he said. "You realize your project's due Friday, though, not today."

Mathis looked at the notebook he'd finished three days early, then at the stack of novels he'd actually come to the library for. "Arno," he said, "hide those before he sees them."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
On the bus to Camp Wabanaki, Hudson held his duffel bag on his lap like a shield and told himself the lump in his throat was allergies. He had never slept away from home for more than one night, and one night had been plenty. Now he faced fourteen of them. When the bus crunched onto the gravel road, a girl across the aisle leaned over.

"You look like you're being donated to the camp against your will," she said. "I'm Delilah. First year?"

"First everything," Hudson said, and she laughed, which somehow made the lump smaller.

Their counselor walked them past the dining hall toward the cabins, but Hudson slowed at a wooden plaque near a big flat rock. He read it twice. The camp had begun in 1861, when a Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, and it was usually considered the first organized American summer camp. Hudson had assumed camps were invented, like, forty years ago, maybe by somebody's grandfather with a whistle. A hundred and sixty years of kids standing on this same rock, and they had all survived.

"Read the plaque, homesick already?" said a boy named Alexe, poking his shoulder. "Historical. Anyway, want to hear the real mystery?"

Alexe lowered his voice. Every morning since staff week, food had vanished from Cabin Four. Granola bars, a bag of pretzels, an entire jar of peanut butter. Nobody confessed. The counselor called it "critters," but Alexe didn't buy it.

Hudson did buy it, at first. But on the second night, lying awake in the dark, he turned the facts over. Raccoons make a mess, and the wrappers in the trash can outside were folded neatly, stacked like origami. Raccoons don't fold. Whoever took the food was careful, quiet, and hungry enough to repeat the crime on a schedule: only after lights-out, only from the cabin whose porch light was burnt out. A pattern. A hidden cause. He just needed to see it.

On Thursday he set his trap. He left half a sleeve of crackers on the floor by the door, then smeared a thin line of peanut butter across the doorstep, low, where a shoe would catch it. He told no one, not even Delilah, and lay in his sleeping bag with his heart going like a drum solo.

Around one in the morning he heard the cabin door ease open. Footsteps. A flashlight clicked on, small and careful. Hudson counted to ten, then sat up. "The peanut butter's on your shoe," he said.

The flashlight swung around and landed on Alexe's face, which had a cracker in it.

"Okay, fine," Alexe whispered. "It's me. My dad lost his job in the recession and money's been tight, so I brought basically no snacks, and everyone else has this giant stable pile of food, and I got hungry." He looked at his sneaker, where the smudge of peanut butter gleamed. "How'd you know it was a person?"

"The wrappers were folded," Hudson said. "Raccoons don't do origami."

Delilah's voice floated from the top bunk. "I knew it was Alexe on day one. He said the camp store was too expensive, then bought two sodas."

Alexe groaned and held out the sleeve of crackers. "Share?"

Hudson took one, because his throat-lump had come back, this time from laughing. Outside, an owl called, and somewhere down the hill the old flat rock sat under the moon, the same rock where a schoolmaster's students had probably stood with their own duffel bags in 1861.

"Tomorrow I'll donate some of my snacks to the cause," Hudson said.

"Already donated," said Delilah, and dropped a granola bar off the top bunk into Alexe's hands.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
story:
Zachary stood in front of the mall's bank kiosk with a birthday cheque for one hundred dollars in his pocket and a problem he could not stop turning over. His grandfather had made an offer at Sunday dinner, before the cake: hand over a thousand dollars of savings, and Grandpa would hold it for five years at five percent simple interest. Zachary had said "sounds good" the way you say it when you have no idea what you're agreeing to.

Simple interest was the part that bothered him. The word sat wrong, like a "free" parking lot that charged by the hour. So he had texted Darcy, who was already at the mall arguing with Milla over which frozen yogurt topping counted as fruit, and now the three of them were gathered around the little wooden table outside the yogurt shop with napkins, a pen Milla had stolen from the bank kiosk, and Zachary's phone calculator.

"Okay," Zachary said. "Five percent of a thousand is fifty a year. Grandpa said the interest doesn't pile up on itself. That's what simple means. So each year it's just another fifty." He wrote 50, 50, 50, 50, 50 down a napkin and added them up. "Twelve fifty. After five years, the account holds one thousand two hundred fifty dollars."

"That's it?" Milla said, sucking froyo off her spoon. "Two hundred fifty total. That seems small."

"It is small," Darcy said. "That's the trap. My cousin had an account where the interest earned interest too, and it ended up with more than the simple version would. Not way more, but more. Like the difference between a plant and a parasite that feeds itself."

"Compound," Ms. Karimi said. Zachary hadn't noticed her; his math teacher was next in line for yogurt, and she was looking at the napkin stack with the mild interest of someone grading homework she hadn't assigned. "You've illustrated the difference on three napkins. I'd give that a B plus for presentation."

"So simple is the worse deal," Zachary said. "Equivalent amounts, same rate, and it still loses?"

"Over five years, it does," Ms. Karimi said, and moved up in line.

Flashback, then: Sunday, Grandpa sliding the cheque across the table with that patient smile, the one he wore whenever he thought he was teaching Zachary something. Zachary, in the present, understood that the smile had been an offer of a lesson, not a trick. The trick would have been accepting it without doing the napkin math.

He texted his grandfather right there. Deal, but can we talk about compound before I sign anything? The reply came before Milla finished her toppings: About time you asked.

Zachary pocketed his birthday cheque and looked at the napkins. "I'm keeping these," he told the others, folding the fifty-times-five one into his jacket like it was a receipt for two hundred fifty dollars he hadn't earned yet.
